SEC Adopts Amendments to Form 10-K Climate Disclosure Requirements

Published 2026-10-07 04:00 UTC

The Securities and Exchange Commission today adopted amendments to its climate-related disclosure requirements for annual reports on Form 10-K. The amendments are intended to simplify reporting for smaller filers while retaining disclosures that investors have said are useful.

Under the amendments, smaller reporting companies and emerging growth companies will be exempt from the requirement to disclose greenhouse gas emissions. They will still be required to describe material climate-related risks and how those risks are managed, but they may provide the information in a narrative form rather than using detailed templates.

Larger companies will continue to provide emissions disclosures, though the amendments extend the phase-in period for third-party assurance by two years. The Commission said the extension responds to comments about the limited availability of qualified assurance providers and the costs of building internal controls.

The amendments also clarify that companies may use reasonable estimates when precise data is unavailable, provided they disclose the methods and assumptions used. A safe harbor protects certain forward-looking statements about transition plans and climate-related targets.

The Commission estimates that the changes will reduce compliance costs for smaller filers by an average of $180,000 per year. Commissioners voted 3-2 to adopt the amendments, with two commissioners issuing statements in dissent arguing that the changes reduce information available to investors.

The amendments will become effective 60 days after publication in the Federal Register. A fact sheet and the adopting release are available on the SEC's website, along with statements from each commissioner.

The Commission also directed staff to review the effects of the amendments after three years and to report on how investors use the disclosures. Companies with questions about the new requirements may contact the Division of Corporation Finance's Office of Chief Counsel, which plans to publish answers to frequently asked questions before the first filings are due.
